title: Week 126 · Lesson 150: Geriatric Primary Care Capstone — Multimorbidity, Prioritization & Goal-Concordant Care
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 126 — Lesson 150: Geriatric Primary Care Capstone

FNP-level goal: Build one coherent care plan for an older adult whose diseases, medicines, function, cognition, caregivers, prognosis, and living environment interact; prioritize immediate danger and patient-important outcomes; apply evidence without mechanically stacking single-disease guidelines; and coordinate care that is beneficial, feasible, and consistent with what matters most.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish multimorbidity from a simple disease list and construct an integrated clinical problem representation.
  • Elicit patient priorities and translate them into measurable health and function goals.
  • Interpret evidence through applicability, absolute benefit, time to benefit, prognosis, competing risk, harms, and treatment burden.
  • Prioritize urgent threats, symptomatic and functional problems, disease modification, prevention, medications, and caregiver-system needs.
  • Create a coordinated, closed-loop plan that preserves autonomy, identifies escalation thresholds, and adapts as health changes.

Part 1 — Multimorbidity Is the Usual Clinical Reality

Multimorbidity generally means two or more chronic physical or mental health conditions, but the clinical burden also includes frailty, disability, geriatric syndromes, social risk, and treatment complexity. Conditions interact: treatment for one disease can worsen another or exceed the patient's capacity to manage it.

The task is not to decide which diagnosis is real. It is to understand which problems drive danger, symptoms, function, and burden today and which interventions produce the greatest net benefit for this person.

Part 2 — Comorbidity Versus Multimorbidity Thinking

Comorbidity thinking chooses an index disease and treats other conditions as modifiers. Multimorbidity thinking has no automatic center; heart failure, CKD, arthritis, depression, cognition, and caregiving may all shape the plan.

This prevents a cardiology target from silently overriding fall safety, or a diabetes metric from overriding recurrent hypoglycemia. Specialists contribute essential expertise, while primary care integrates the whole plan.

Part 3 — Start With an Integrated Problem Representation

Summarize age and context, baseline and current function, major active conditions, recent trajectory, cognition, medications, living situation, caregiver, and the patient's priority. Include instability and uncertainty.

For example: An 84-year-old living alone with HFpEF, CKD, diabetes, mild cognitive impairment, recurrent falls, orthostasis, and recent hospitalization wants to remain home but cannot reliably manage a complex medication schedule. This representation directs care more effectively than an unranked diagnosis list.

Part 4 — Immediate Danger Comes First

Before long-term optimization, identify acute threats: chest pain, severe dyspnea, stroke signs, sepsis, major bleeding, hypoglycemia, delirium, fracture, medication toxicity, suicidal risk, abuse, unsafe discharge, or inability to meet basic needs.

Goal-concordant care does not mean routine outpatient management of instability. Clarify emergency preferences and orders, but treat acute danger according to capacity, known goals, and appropriate emergency standards.

Part 5 — Ask What Matters Most

Ask what the patient most wants to be able to do and what they most want to avoid. Staying in one's home is broad; the actionable goal may be walking safely to the bathroom, attending worship, staying alert for grandchildren, or avoiding another hospitalization.

Ask which symptoms or treatments interfere most. A patient may rank dizziness above knee pain, or caregiver independence above a small long-term risk reduction. Preferences guide decisions but do not replace clear clinical recommendations.

Part 6 — Convert Values Into Health Priorities

A value such as independence becomes a health outcome: safe transfer, preserved cognition, continence, medication simplicity, and reliable support. A value such as longevity requires clarification of acceptable burden and function.

Document one to three priorities and link each intervention to them. If a treatment cannot be connected to a meaningful outcome, its purpose should be reexamined.

Part 7 — Use the Geriatric Domains Together

Integrate mind, mobility, medications, multicomplexity, and matters most. Add nutrition, sensory function, living environment, social connection, caregiver capacity, and advance planning. These domains are not separate checkboxes.

For example, hearing loss can lower cognitive test performance, misunderstanding can cause medication error, error can cause fall, and the fall can lead to hospitalization and delirium. One intervention may improve several domains.

Part 8 — Atypical Presentation Is Common but Not Universal

Older adults may present with delirium, falls, weakness, anorexia, or functional decline rather than classic disease-specific symptoms. Infection may occur without prominent fever; myocardial ischemia may present with dyspnea or fatigue.

Do not attribute every nonspecific symptom to aging. Atypical presentation should broaden mechanism-based evaluation, not justify indiscriminate testing or diagnostic nihilism.

Part 9 — Establish the Trajectory

Ask what changed over hours, days, months, and years. Identify sentinel events such as hospitalization, bereavement, fall, medication change, move, or caregiver loss. Compare current ADLs and IADLs with baseline.

Trajectory helps distinguish acute reversible illness, post-hospital vulnerability, progressive disease, and chronic adaptation. It also informs prognosis and urgency.

Part 10 — Interpret Evidence for This Patient

Ask whether study participants resembled the patient in age, frailty, cognition, kidney function, comorbidities, and baseline risk. A relative risk reduction may look impressive while absolute benefit is small. Trials may underrepresent the people most likely to experience treatment harm.

Consider the outcome measured. A laboratory target may not translate into better function or survival. Explain evidence strength and uncertainty without pretending that no evidence means no decision.

Part 11 — Time to Benefit

Preventive interventions differ in how long benefit takes to emerge. Compare that time with the patient's likely health trajectory, treatment burden, and goals. Prognosis includes function and quality of life, not only life expectancy.

A long-horizon screening or preventive drug may offer little value to a patient with limited prognosis and high burden, while vaccination, fall prevention, symptom treatment, or blood-pressure safety may provide near-term benefit. Do not use age alone as the cutoff.

Part 12 — Competing Risks

A patient can be at high disease-specific risk but more likely to experience another outcome first. Competing mortality, functional decline, bleeding, falls, or treatment intolerance may reduce the value of an intervention.

This does not make prevention meaningless. It changes absolute benefit, priority, and how options should be discussed.

Part 13 — Treatment Burden

Treatment burden includes pill count, dosing, monitoring, injections, equipment, appointments, transportation, dietary rules, cost, adverse effects, and the work placed on caregivers. Burden is not inconvenience; it can determine whether essential care succeeds.

Ask how many hours per week care requires and what the patient skips. A perfect plan that cannot be performed is unsafe. Simplify while protecting the highest-value components.

Part 14 — Patient Capacity for Self-Management

Assess cognition, health literacy, language, hearing, vision, dexterity, mobility, finances, pharmacy access, digital access, and support. Capacity to make a decision differs from ability to execute a complex plan.

Use pill packaging, one pharmacy, synchronized refills, home nursing, caregiver teaching, accessible devices, and written plans. If support cannot bridge the gap, reconsider the treatment or living setting.

Part 15 — Guidelines Can Conflict

Single-disease guidelines may produce incompatible targets, diets, or medicines when stacked. Diuresis can worsen kidney function and orthostasis; tight glycemic treatment can cause hypoglycemia; anticoagulation can conflict with bleeding; pain treatment can worsen cognition.

Identify the conflict explicitly, estimate the consequences of each option, and make one integrated recommendation. Do not leave the patient to reconcile specialists alone.

Part 16 — Prioritize the Care Plan

  1. Immediate threats and reversible instability.
  2. Symptoms or syndromes causing suffering and unsafe function.
  3. High-value disease treatment with near-term or substantial benefit.
  4. Prevention appropriate to risk, prognosis, and time to benefit.
  5. Treatment simplification, social supports, and future planning.

Priority is dynamic. A stable preventive issue may move forward after delirium, falls, or medication harm is controlled.

Part 17 — Medication Optimization

For every medicine, identify indication, target, expected benefit, time to benefit, dose, kidney and liver fit, interactions, burden, and monitoring. Look for underuse as well as overuse. Deprescribing should not become withholding beneficial treatment from older adults.

Use Lesson 142: remove no-indication, duplicate, harmful, or goal-discordant therapy; taper when needed; add alternatives; and follow withdrawal and disease recurrence. Preserve the medicines that clearly support current priorities.

Part 18 — Individualize Targets

Blood pressure, glucose, lipid, anticoagulation, weight, and pain plans should reflect baseline risk, organ function, falls, hypoglycemia, symptoms, cognition, and goals. Individualization is not abandonment of measurement.

Define a target range or clinical outcome and the reason for it. Avoid vague statements such as less strict without a monitoring and escalation plan.

Part 19 — Screening and Prevention

Review vaccination, tobacco, physical activity, nutrition, osteoporosis, falls, sensory care, dental health, mood, and social connection. Cancer and other screening decisions should incorporate prior results, risk, willingness for downstream testing and treatment, prognosis, and time to benefit.

Do not screen when the patient would decline or cannot benefit from the diagnostic and treatment cascade. Do not stop useful prevention solely because of chronological age.

Part 20 — Diagnostic Stewardship

Before ordering a test, ask what question it answers, how the result changes management, what false positives or incidental findings may trigger, and whether the patient would pursue the next step. Under-testing and over-testing both cause harm.

Prioritize tests that identify reversible danger or materially change a goal-concordant plan. Explain when watchful waiting is active monitoring rather than neglect.

Part 21 — Function Is an Outcome

Track ADLs, IADLs, gait, transfers, endurance, falls, and participation. A treatment that improves a laboratory value but worsens dizziness, cognition, or mobility may have negative net value.

Use rehabilitation, assistive devices, home modification, pain treatment, and caregiver support to preserve participation. Ask whether the patient can do the activity they identified as most important.

Part 22 — Cognition, Capacity, and Future Planning

Screen when concern exists and distinguish delirium from chronic change. Assess decision-specific capacity and optimize sensory and language access. Involve the chosen caregiver or proxy with permission.

Complete advance care planning while the patient can participate. Ensure proxy and portable orders are accessible. The care plan should anticipate what happens if cognition or function worsens.

Part 23 — Caregiver Is Part of the Care System

Assess caregiver health, sleep, mood, finances, skills, willingness, conflict, respite, and other responsibilities. Caregiver strain can cause medication errors, hospitalization, or unsafe care even when devotion is strong.

Offer training, respite, home services, adult day care, social work, and realistic transitions. Protect against mistreatment or exploitation when warning signs appear.

Part 24 — Social and Structural Context

Housing, food, utilities, transportation, neighborhood safety, discrimination, language, rural access, immigration concerns, insurance, and digital systems shape outcomes. Social risk is not a patient failure.

Partner with community health workers, social services, legal aid, benefits programs, pharmacists, and care managers. Track whether the resource connected and solved the barrier.

Part 25 — One Coordinated Plan

Name a primary coordinator and define each specialist's role. Maintain one medication list, problem list, priority statement, and monitoring calendar. Resolve conflicting recommendations directly between clinicians.

At every transition, transfer baseline cognition and function, goals, proxy, pending results, medication rationale, and red flags. Coordination is a clinical intervention.

Part 26 — Shared Decision-Making With a Recommendation

Explain options, likely outcomes, uncertainties, and burdens in plain language. Ask how the patient wants decisions made and whom to involve. Then offer professional guidance connected to priorities.

Shared decision-making does not require the patient to choose alone from a menu. A clear recommendation can reduce burden while preserving autonomy.

Part 27 — Time-Limited Trials

For uncertain benefit, define a trial, duration, measurable target, adverse-effect threshold, follow-up owner, and stop or continue rule. Examples include a new pain strategy, rehabilitation, medication reduction, or disease-directed therapy.

Measure the patient's priority outcome, not only the biomarker. A trial without reassessment becomes indefinite treatment.

Part 28 — When to Refer to Geriatrics

Consider geriatrics consultation for severe multimorbidity, frailty, recurrent falls, polypharmacy, difficult capacity questions, behavioral symptoms, unexplained functional decline, caregiver crisis, or conflicting goals and treatments.

Limited specialist access does not prevent the FNP from applying geriatric principles. Use interdisciplinary resources and teleconsultation when available.

Part 29 — Palliative Care and Hospice

Palliative care can accompany treatment when symptoms, serious-illness decisions, or caregiver burden are complex. Hospice is appropriate for eligible terminal illness when comfort-focused goals align with the benefit.

Referral is not giving up. It adds symptom, communication, spiritual, and caregiver expertise. Continue primary-care continuity when possible.

Part 30 — Red Flags and Escalation

Emergency evaluation is required for acute neurologic change, severe dyspnea or chest pain, major bleeding, severe hypoglycemia, sepsis, fracture, overdose, suicidal danger, abuse with imminent threat, or inability to maintain essential safety.

Urgent reassessment is appropriate for new delirium, rapid weight or functional loss, recurrent falls, worsening medication errors, rising caregiver strain, or a plan that can no longer be performed. Do not allow the complexity of multimorbidity to normalize acute deterioration.

Part 31 — Measure Success

Success may include fewer falls, clearer thinking, stable volume, less pain, simpler medicines, completed appointments, caregiver sleep, staying home safely, or fewer unwanted hospitalizations. Disease metrics remain useful but are not the entire outcome.

Track the priorities chosen with the patient and revisit them after major events. Improvement in one domain can reveal a new priority in another.

Part 32 — Phase 5 Integration

Reproductive, pregnancy, postpartum, newborn, pediatric, adolescent, and geriatric care all require age- and context-specific safety. Across the lifespan, the FNP integrates prevention, development, family systems, capacity, medication, function, culture, and access.

Lesson 150 closes Phase 5 by making integration itself the skill: one person, one family context, many conditions, and one coherent care plan.

Clinical Case 1 — The Guideline Collision

An 84-year-old with HFpEF, CKD, diabetes, mild cognitive impairment, orthostasis, and falls takes 14 medicines. The patient's priority is walking safely at home. The FNP first excludes acute danger, reconciles medicines, reduces hypoglycemia and orthostatic burden, preserves high-value heart and kidney therapy where tolerated, arranges strength and home support, and defines monitoring rather than applying every disease target independently.

Clinical Case 2 — Screening and Time to Benefit

An 88-year-old with advanced frailty and limited life expectancy is scheduled for screening that would lead to invasive workup the patient would not accept. The FNP discusses expected benefit horizon, downstream burden, prognosis, and values, recommends stopping that screening, and redirects attention to vaccination, falls, symptoms, vision, and caregiver support that offer nearer benefit.

Clinical Case 3 — Conflicting Specialist Plans

A patient receives one instruction to increase diuresis and another to increase fluids after kidney decline, while dizziness and edema worsen. The FNP obtains current examination and labs, contacts the specialists, clarifies the dominant physiology and goals, creates one written volume and medication plan, assigns follow-up ownership, and prevents the patient from arbitrating contradictory advice.

FNP High-Yield Framework: PRIORITY

  1. P — Protect from immediate harm: acute illness, medication toxicity, unsafe function, abuse.
  2. R — Represent the whole patient: diseases, trajectory, function, mind, supports, environment.
  3. I — Identify what matters: activities, fears, acceptable burden, outcomes, decision style.
  4. O — Open the evidence: applicability, absolute benefit, harm, prognosis, time to benefit.
  5. R — Reconcile treatment: guideline conflicts, medicines, tests, appointments, feasibility.
  6. I — Integrate one plan: ranked goals, team roles, caregiver, services, monitoring.
  7. T — Trial and track: measurable outcomes, time limit, adverse thresholds, closed loops.
  8. Y — Yield and revise: respond to changing health, preferences, capacity, and care setting.

Take-Home Summary

Multimorbidity care is not the sum of separate guidelines. FNP-level integration begins with immediate safety and what matters most, interprets evidence through absolute benefit, prognosis, time to benefit, harms, and burden, and creates a feasible plan that preserves function and autonomy. The best plan is coherent enough for the patient, caregiver, pharmacy, specialists, and next care setting to follow together.

Educational note: Apply current AGS multimorbidity principles, AHRQ multiple-chronic-condition resources, disease-specific guidelines, NIA geriatric guidance, state scope, payer, capacity, reporting, and emergency protocols. Multimorbidity does not make acute danger routine; sudden decline, unstable illness, serious medication harm, unsafe care, or immediate threat requires prompt escalation.
